Round 8 answer to L5-6: accept. There is no event mechanism anywhere in the requirements and none was asked for. The reasoning is the rule this design has now applied four times: naming an event with no subscriber is a mechanism with no reader. If a subscriber appears later the events can be named then, against a real consumer.

R-8 · human — The transport adapter family inherits the four existing normalized answer shapes and their exit codes unchanged. No transport vocabulary crosses the boundary.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 8 answer to L5-7: accept. This is the anti-corruption layer the layer asks for, and it was already the reason an earlier round made transport a fifth adapter family rather than a switch. A pane identifier, a terminal identifier and a subagent handle all arrive in the same shape, and nothing above the boundary learns which transport it is talking to. Cite ADAPTERS.md:27-38.

Round R-7

R-7 · human — The waiter is built and the capability is declared, with a conformance probe for each supported harness. Where the probe fails, the design degrades to the contact agent checking on its next turn and says so.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 7 answer to L4-10: declare-it, with no note attached. This resolves the steer conflict surfaced in the same round in favour of the written rule, which requires capability needs to be declared. The price the human accepted is stated on the card and is not softened here: this feature now edits two shared contracts it does not own, the capability table and the conformance ledger, which is real scope growth for a resumption nicety. What it buys is that a parked agent failing to wake on another harness is reported rather than silent. L4 closes with this card.

Round R-6

R-6 · human — HL-3 Authorization and data scoping is signed: every protected surface with its permitted and denied roles and what actually enforces each, the scoping mechanism for both records, and the three rules nothing can enforce.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 6 answer to HL3-1: sign, with no note attached, so the quote is the mark itself. No approving sentence was written and none is invented here. The packet stated plainly that six of the nine surface rows are enforced by nothing, so a violation is first noticed by a human reading a diff, and that one row is unenforceable in principle because a file read is invisible to hooks and no mechanism could be built for it without a new harness capability. Signing accepted those five risks. The two strongest controls in the table are not this plugin's: merge is guarded by the forge, and the pre-commit gate refuses an agent commit while letting a human through.

R-6 · human — A parked agent is resumed automatically. A background waiter is armed at park time and its exit wakes the contact agent.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 6 answer to L4-9: waker-undeclared, chosen over the agent's recommendation and over the agent's stated strongest objection. Recorded as given. The mechanism is real and documented: DELEGATION.md:34 states that only completion re-invokes a waiting orchestrator, and hooks/stall-watchdog.sh:2-6 states that its exit is the wake-up. What the human accepted with this option is that the capability behind it is undeclared: CAPABILITIES.md:5-22 lists sixteen capabilities and names no background, notification or resumption capability, and providers/CONFORMANCE.md:13-34 carries no probe for it on either harness. The agent surfaced one further consequence in round 7 rather than acting on it: this choice contradicts a written rule in the repository's own steering file, which requires capability needs to be declared. Whether the waiter is declared or not is settled by that card, and every option there still builds this waiter.

Round R-5

R-5 · human — The access policy keeps every row and gains a column naming what actually enforces it. Most rows read convention. Nothing new is built to enforce agent identity.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 5 answer to L4-1: label-each-row. Taken against a verified finding that no agent identity reaches any hook, that a file read cannot be observed at all because the read tool is outside the shared matcher set, and that every single-writer rule in this plugin is prose with no enforcing script. The ruling keeps design intent on the record where a reviewer can check against it, and refuses to let the document imply a guard that does not exist. The rejected alternatives were narrowing the policy to what a binary agent-or-human signal can enforce, and building the first role-keyed runtime check this plugin has ever had.

R-5 · human — Who resumes a parked agent was re-asked as L4-9 in round 6 and settled in round 11 as S-38: the background waiter is dropped, and the contact agent resumes a parked agent when it next checks the manifest.

What settled it
Evidence
Asked in round 5 and answered with a write-in asking for an argument, which is not a choice, so the card stayed open and L4-9 re-asked it. Round 6 chose an automatic waiter, round 7 declared it as a capability, and round 11 reversed to contact-checks once the waiter was shown to die with the session that armed it. This card sat under still-open on the page until round 21, although S-38 had answered it; it is closed here so the page stops showing a settled question as open.

R-5 · human — A run reports through the existing reporting protocol, unchanged.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 5 answer to L4-3: accept. A second reporting style would be a second home for the rule and the two would drift. The weighed alternative, a purpose-built format for a team of agents, lost on that ground.

R-5 · human — Each transport verb declares its own time budget and whether repeating it is safe. Nothing retries automatically.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 5 answer to L4-4: accept. This was already inside the HL-2 signature from round 2, so the row confirmed rather than decided. The weighed alternative, one central retry policy applied by the dispatcher, lost because repeating a verb that starts a process starts a second process.

R-5 · human — No transport verb carries an idempotency key.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 5 answer to L4-5: accept. An idempotency key exists to make a repeat safe and nothing here repeats without a caller deciding to, so keys would be machinery with no trigger. Consistent with the house answer: zero declarations of idempotency, timeout or retry across the adapter families. The weighed alternative, a key on the start verb, lost because it needs a second store to remember keys while the manifest already records what is running.

R-5 · human — The feature handles no secret. It names models and transports in configuration and never reads, stores or passes a credential.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 5 answer to L4-6: accept. Credentials already have a home and an owner in this plugin. The weighed alternative, a per-role credential so cheap roles could use a cheaper account, lost because it would put secrets into a manifest that is written to disk and read by a dashboard.

R-5 · human — The topology map is the switch. A stage with no entry in it runs exactly as it does today.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 5 answer to L4-7: accept. The map that already decides the pattern per stage can say no pattern, so a separate flag would be a second source of truth to keep in step. The weighed alternative, one global switch for the whole feature, lost on that ground while being acknowledged as the blunt instrument you want when something is badly wrong.

R-5 · human — Everything is a short call. Waiting is done by polling the status verb, never by a blocking wait inside a verb.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 5 answer to L4-8: accept. Already inside the HL-2 signature, and recorded there as the agent's least confident recommendation. The weighed alternative, adding a verb that blocks until an agent finishes, was flagged on the card as voiding the HL-2 signature and re-packeting the verb set; the human did not reopen it.

Round R-4

R-4 · human — HL-1 Persistence is signed: the run manifest file, one agent entry, one knowledge-store entry, and the identity, concurrency, retention and evolution table, exactly as the packet stated them.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 4 answer to HL1-1: sign, with no note attached, so the quote is the mark itself. No approving sentence was written and none is invented here. Signing settled three rows the packet marked as the agent's rather than quoted from a criterion, because the requirements were silent on each: the process identifier, without which AC-013 cannot kill anything it names; a proposed meaning for the word ground, which AC-018 uses once and never defines; and manifest retention, which no criterion states. It also took as accepted the six risks the packet listed. Any later layer that moves a row voids this signature and the packet returns marked with the delta.

R-4 · human — Environment facts are re-detected each run. Nothing about the machine is promoted to any durable register before the knowledge store is deleted.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 4 answer to L3-6: drop-promotion. This removes a clause from AC-019, which is why it was never the agent's to take. It is consistent with the earlier decision that detection reads the session it is in rather than the machine, on the grounds that what is installed and what is usable are different questions. The alternative the human had proposed in round 3, promoting facts into the layered steering file, was weighed on the card and lost on two counts: the fact would be prose an agent reads rather than data a program reads, and every promotion would cost a human approval, so an unattended run could promote nothing.

Round R-3

R-3 · human — The run manifest is keyed by feature alone. The owning contact session is a field inside it, which adoption rewrites.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 3 answer to L3-3: feature-only. This is a ruling on a requirement contradiction, not a design preference. AC-012 keys the manifest by feature identifier and contact session; AC-015 requires a later contact agent to adopt that manifest rather than start a second one. A key holding the old session never matches a new one, so the two could not both hold. The ruling keeps AC-015 whole and edits the key in AC-012, which now reads as an attribute rather than part of the key.

R-3 · human — AC-019's promotion clause is dropped. Environment facts are re-detected each run and nothing about a machine is carried forward.

What settled it
Evidence
Asked in round 3, answered in round 4 as card L3-6: drop-promotion. It stayed open across one round on purpose. The round 3 answer was a write-in naming the repository's layered context harness as the durable register, which contradicted a claim the agent had made. Rather than apply it or dismiss it, the claim was checked and the card re-asked with what the check found. The human was right that the harness is real, layered and stewarded with their own approval on every write. The agent was right that no section shape in it holds a machine fact and that no script reads those files back as data. One part of the write-in was wrong and was corrected on the card: the Codex-side file is not a write target, because no skill writes it.

R-3 · agent — The knowledge store is deleted by the same explicit cleanup step that closes the desktop tool terminals, rather than by a new trigger of its own.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 3 answer to L3-5: accept, audited. The step it rides on already exists for another reason, so this adds an action rather than a trigger. The accepted loss is on the record and unchanged: a session that is killed never reaches the step, so the store survives until the next run for that feature overwrites it.
Audit
explicit

Round R-2

R-2 · human — The transport verb set is signed: six verbs, inherited answer shapes, a declared time budget and repeat behaviour per verb, and input as a positional argument.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 2 answer to HL2-1: sign, with no note attached, so the quote is the mark itself. No approving sentence was written and none is invented here. Signing took as accepted the four risks the packet named and its three weighed alternatives, including the one the agent named as its least confident: polling for status rather than a blocking wait verb. Any later change to the verb set voids this signature and it is re-packeted.

R-2 · human — The run manifest and the knowledge store live under the ignored agent directory, keyed by feature.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 2 answer to L3-1: agent-dir. It was a call rather than a recommendation because the alternative needed a new ignore rule for the documentation tree, and ignore rules are repository configuration that this feature's own access policy forbids any agent to write.

R-2 · agent — The manifest is written under a directory mutex and replaced by writing a temporary file and renaming it, so no reader sees a half-written kill list.

What settled it
Evidence
Both halves are existing house patterns: maven-lock.sh:1-65 is a directory mutex with stale-lock theft and exit traps, and gate-cache.sh:83-93 writes temp-then-rename with a comment saying the purpose is to stop a reader seeing a torn key. Accepted in round 2.
Audit
explicit

Round R-1

R-1 · human — A run outlives its contact session. A later contact agent adopts it by feature id plus contact session and continues the work.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 1 answer to L1-1: durable-run, no note. This closed session-end teardown as an option before card L2-2 was reached, because a run meant to survive its session must not be ended by the session ending.

R-1 · agent — The plugin starts and owns processes the harness does not know about, each wrapped in an operating-system job whose close ends the whole tree.

What settled it
Evidence
Requirement decision 0007 states that registration alone is not cleanup. A live trial on this machine killed a parent and watched its child and grandchild keep running, so the job object is the guarantee and the manifest is the report. Accepted in round 1.
Audit
explicit

R-1 · human — Layer one is otherwise inherited: one machine, local only, nothing added to the deployment model.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 1 answer to L1-3: accept. Every transport in the catalog starts a local process, a local pane or a local terminal, and none needs a port or a second host.

R-1 · agent — Transport becomes a fifth adapter family, one kind per transport, beside tracker, forge, notes and build gate.

What settled it
Evidence
The registry check derives families from the adapters directory listing at adapter_registry_check.py:41-46, and the dispatcher builds its path from the family string with no set check at adapter.sh:37-52. Only scripts/afk-config.py and CONFIG.md must change. Accepted in round 1.
Audit
explicit

R-1 · human — Teardown is the operating-system job, not a cleanup step. An explicit close runs only for the desktop tool's terminals, which a job cannot hold.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 1 answer to L2-2: job-is-the-guarantee. The accepted cost is recorded rather than hidden — a killed session kills its agents and leaves nobody to report what could not be killed, which is a known loss against AC-013.

R-1 · human — A stage learns its pattern from one central map held in configuration, keyed by stage name.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 1 answer to L2-3: central-map. The consequence accepted with it is that this feature edits skills it does not own, and the map is the single home for the topology.

R-1 · human — All six human-locked aspects are live for this feature. None was argued down to not-applicable.

What settled it
Evidence
Round 1 answer to L2-4: accept. The two escapable ones were kept live on purpose: the run manifest is read back after its writer is gone, and the transport verb set is a contract other people write adapters against.

"fork": "Layer eight is the tactical patterns: the shapes the code takes, which matter here only because they decide what an executor implements against.

Both real cards below came out of grounding the layer rather than out of a catalogue, and both are about copying something this plugin already does or deliberately not copying it.

The first is the one I care most about. You signed a lifecycle three rounds ago with an explicit column saying which state may follow which. I went looking for how this plugin enforces such a thing, and the answer is that it does not. The existing status set is checked for membership only: nothing reads the current value before writing, so a jump straight from the first state to the last would pass unnoticed. The ordering is held by the order of steps in prose.

I re-checked that myself rather than trust it, because it decides the card. Confirmed: only five files touch those status tokens, and every hit for transition logic belongs to the tracker adapters, where the state machine is the external tracker's and this plugin merely calls it. There is no in-house machine to imitate.

So the question is whether the column you signed gets enforced or stays prose like everything around it.

The second card is a fork I did not expect to find. This plugin has two different ways of choosing an implementation, not one. Adapters are chosen by a key in the repository's configuration. Harnesses are chosen by asking each candidate whether it is active and taking the highest priority among those that say yes. You put the transport in an adapter family last round, which points at the first mechanism — but what varies for a transport is the machine, and the configuration file is per repository. That mismatch is the card.",

nodes.evidence: A pattern is a reusable team shape. It knows nothing of the workflow; its description says how and when it is useful. The contact agent reads the descriptions and proposes patterns for the task, possibly several combined, and the human picks. The plugin ships five built-in patterns and no stage map. Every pattern that starts agents meets the **pattern standard** (the 4 properties PS-1 to PS-4): duties kept apart, independent checks, several angles on a problem, and maximum autonomy. Inside a team, agents message each other directly along the talk edges the pattern declares. A role's result goes to its **report target** (the agent named to receive it), by default the agent that asked for the role (ADR-0015). The contact agent gets a copy of each finished, parked and exited message to keep the manifest. It reads a result only when it is the target.
| PS-1 | Segregation of duty | The role that produces a piece of work never checks it |
| PS-2 | Independent cross-check and audit | At least 1 agent that did not produce a piece of work checks it, and each checker writes its first findings before it sees another checker's |
| PS-3 | Several angles on a problem | A problem that needs thinking gets at least 2 agents that differ in model or in brief |
| PS-4 | Maximum autonomy | The team runs to its end without the human, stops only at the stops its description names, and decides and records everything else |

claims.text: GLOSSARY.md:38 at HEAD already lists the charter in a Team pattern's data, so the plan 0005 context excerpt and SDD §14 landmine saying the entry has no charter is stale at this head.

.gitignore at HEAD ignores directories named build, dist, lib (hooks/lib/ re-included), var and env, files named MANIFEST or *.key, and secrets/, so a record or charter file under such a name is never tracked.

A resolver that imports only the Python standard library changes neither runtime/pyproject.toml nor uv.lock nor P1's pins; a new third-party import needs a pin there and the FRESHNESS.md runtime/ row.
Both plugin manifests list skills (and the Claude one agents) only; the new scripts/team/ files ship inside the tree a harness copies verbatim, with no manifest entry.

Dispatch and module loading at the declared B3, B5 and B10 sites reach no pattern: adapter.sh resolves only adapters/<family>/<kind> and HEAD has no transport or pattern family, tracker_api.py and the tracker MCP server load the configuration reader and read only tracker.
